How pictures teach us to see A painting consists of marks on a surface. Yet we see a face, sunlight, or space that seems to extend behind its frame. How does this happen? And why have artists in different periods represented the same world in such different ways?
These questions drive E. H. Gombrich’s Art and Illusion: A Study in the Psychology of Pictorial Representation. First published in 1960, the book grew from his Mellon Lectures. It connects the history of image making with the psychology of perception. Its subject is the construction of convincing appearances, rather than a survey of great works. The publisher’s edition on JSTOR gives the book’s structure and chapter openings.
Gombrich’s central argument has two connected parts. Artists work with learned ways of making images, which they test and change. Viewers bring expectations that help them interpret those images. A convincing picture emerges from the interaction between marks, habits, and recognition.
Schema and correction: a starting point that can change Gombrich calls an artist’s starting pattern a schema. It can be a basic shape, a familiar arrangement, or an established way of drawing a particular kind of thing. The artist adjusts this starting point against the demands of the subject. This process is schema and correction.
Consider an illustrative drawing exercise. You begin a pitcher with an oval opening and a rough outline. Looking again, you find that its neck is narrower than your drawing suggests. You change the outline. The first marks give you something specific to compare with the object. They also make your errors visible.
The schema is therefore useful even when it is wrong. It makes a difficult task manageable. The danger comes when a familiar pattern resists correction. We may draw the object we expect instead of attending to its particular form.
This explains Gombrich’s emphasis on making before matching. Observation works through available means of representation. Michael Podro’s British Academy account of Gombrich explains both the value and the breadth of this model.
Why style cannot be removed by looking harder If artists merely copied what reached their eyes, shared subjects should produce much more similar pictures. Gombrich instead treats style as part of the equipment artists use to represent the world.
In the book’s account of Ludwig Richter, artists draw the same place but produce different results. Their tools, training, and preferences shape their choices. Gombrich uses such cases to challenge the idea of an innocent eye: sight freed from all prior knowledge and habits.
This does not make accuracy impossible. A picture can provide reliable information about a subject. But we must ask what information it is meant to provide. A map, a portrait, and a landscape answer different questions. Each selects relationships from a world too rich for any single image to contain.
His argument leaves room for both convention and correction. A learned style can guide attention without making every result equally accurate. The authorized excerpt in Aesthetics: A Reader in Philosophy of the Arts presents this distinction.
A rhinoceros made from other images Dürer’s rhinoceros is a useful example of how an image can become an authority. Dürer made his woodcut without seeing the animal. He relied on a description and a sketch. The result has convincing weight and detail, but it also has armorlike plates and an extra horn.
The image remained influential because later makers could use it as a ready model. A strong representation can shape what people expect an unfamiliar animal to look like. Its apparent precision may hide the weak basis of some details. The Natural History Museum’s account independently documents the print’s errors and influence.
Read alongside schema and correction, this case suggests a practical warning. Detail does not establish accuracy. When judging an image, ask how its maker obtained the information, and whether later versions checked the subject or simply repeated an earlier picture.
From light into paint Gombrich begins his discussion of likeness with Constable’s Wivenhoe Park. Its sunlight and open space seem natural. That ease can conceal the difficulty of producing the effect.
A painter cannot put outdoor sunlight on a canvas. Paint offers a limited range of brightness. The artist must arrange differences within that range so that we experience light, shadow, and distance. Podro highlights Gombrich’s insistence that the effect depends on relationships between tones, rather than the isolated brightness of individual colors.
An everyday comparison helps explain the problem. A white patch can appear bright against a dark field and dull against a lighter one. Its role changes with its surroundings. Judging the patch alone misses what it does in the whole picture.
For a reader, this changes the question to ask of a painting. Instead of checking each color against a remembered object, examine how the colors work together. Which contrasts create the strongest light? Which edges separate objects? Which soften into atmosphere?
The beholder’s share The viewer supplies what Gombrich calls the beholder’s share. We recognize objects, infer space, and complete information that the artist leaves unstated. A picture offers cues; perception organizes them into a plausible scene.
This contribution becomes easier to notice when the information is incomplete. Gombrich discusses our ability to find forms in clouds and our response to suggestive painted marks. A few brushstrokes can become a landscape once we recognize the arrangement.
In a later clarification, he explains that even an ordinary photograph needs this constructive contribution. We readily recognize trees and buildings, although the photograph cannot establish every branch’s direction or every building’s dimensions. Recognition can feel complete while leaving much unresolved. See his discussion of perception and imagination.
The viewer’s contribution also has limits. We cannot freely decide that every patch means anything at all. The marks and their arrangement constrain a successful reading. In his 1962 response on illusions in painting, Gombrich uses stage scenery to explain how perspective can unsettle our sense of where physical space ends and painted space begins.
Invention, caricature, and expression The book’s later discussion of caricature extends its account of visual discovery. A distorted face can remain recognizable. Representation therefore does not always require a complete inventory of correct measurements. Artists can discover economical ways to suggest identity and expression.
The broader implication is that invention can reveal which cues matter. An artist tries a pictorial effect; the result changes what artists and viewers can notice. Technical skill includes discovering useful departures from literal resemblance.
This helps explain why Gombrich’s subject extends beyond deceptive painting. In his preface to the 2000 edition, he explicitly rejects the assumption that studying illusion means recommending illusionistic art. His question concerns how representation works. Artistic value requires further judgments.
What the argument explains, and where it stops The book offers a strong account of learning within traditions. It explains how inherited methods can enable observation, and how correction can change those methods. It also gives viewers a reason to examine their own expectations.
Its key term is broad, however. A schema can mean a geometric aid, a copied model, or a mental expectation. These are related, but they are not identical. Veronika Kopecky’s study of Gombrich’s correspondence documents questions about this flexibility and the book’s reception.
There are further limits to keep in view. An account of convincing appearances does not fully explain a work’s religious use, political force, or emotional importance. Nor should naturalism become a scale on which every artistic tradition must be ranked. These are limits of the framework’s scope, rather than reasons to dismiss its insights.
For practical use, try looking at one image twice. First identify what you recognize immediately. Then inspect the marks that support that recognition. Compare the two experiences. You may find that something which seemed fully described depends on a few carefully placed cues.
For someone making images, the corresponding exercise is to keep an initial sketch and compare it with later revisions. Identify where you corrected the subject’s shape, and where you changed the image to make its effect clearer. This is an application of Gombrich’s argument, rather than a formal exercise prescribed by the book. It turns his account into a way to study how making and seeing develop together.
Sources Princeton University Press edition on JSTOR: verified title, author, contents, and chapter openings. Authorized Gombrich excerpt in Aesthetics: style, representation, and accuracy. The Gombrich Archive: 2000 preface, perception and imagination, and 1962 reply on illusion: the author’s clarifications. Michael Podro, British Academy memoir, and Veronika Kopecky on the book’s correspondence: scholarly context and limitations. Natural History Museum: Dürer’s rhinoceros: independent evidence for the example.

Artists’ lives as a history of artistic change Giorgio Vasari’s The Lives of the Artists turns biographies into an argument about history. Artists inherit skills, study earlier works, and solve problems that their predecessors could not solve. In Vasari’s account, these advances restore the achievements of ancient art. They eventually produce a modern art that can rival or surpass antiquity.
Vasari was himself a painter and architect. He first published the book in 1550 and issued a much larger edition in 1568. Its fuller title names painters, sculptors, and architects. Modern selections vary in their contents, so a short edition may give only part of his project. The National Gallery’s biography establishes the publication history; Oxford’s edition description outlines the book’s broad structure.
This is also a work of praise, criticism, and storytelling. Vasari wants readers to remember artists as people whose choices matter. His account helped define a lasting picture of the Renaissance, but its judgments come from a committed participant with strong preferences.
Three ages, with perfection as the destination Vasari organizes the lives into three broad ages. They resemble the growth of a person from infancy through youth to maturity.
The first age begins with figures such as Cimabue and Giotto. Vasari credits them with renewing art through closer attention to nature. The second includes Brunelleschi, Donatello, Ghiberti, and Masaccio. These artists develop stronger methods for representing bodies, space, and proportion. The third reaches its highest achievements through Leonardo, Raphael, and above all Michelangelo.
In the preface to the second part, Vasari explains why this division matters. He wants to explain improvement and decline, rather than compile an inventory of works. He also asks readers to judge early artists partly by the obstacles they faced. A modest beginning can deserve praise when the maker had few useful models.
This produces a productive tension. Vasari recognizes that artists work within different conditions. Yet he measures their achievements against an ideal that he locates in his own period. His history gives earlier artists dignity while making them steps toward a later destination.
That destination is his interpretation. Readers do not have to accept it to learn from his comparisons.
Disegno: drawing as thought made visible One idea connects the three arts: disegno. The term includes drawing, but also the understanding and design that drawing expresses. It joins the trained hand to the mind’s judgment of form.
Vasari’s technical introduction makes this connection concrete. Architecture, sculpture, and painting require knowledge of materials and methods. His discussion moves among stone, models, drawing, and ways of applying paint. These are working practices, not merely subjects for abstract praise. The separately translated Vasari on Technique preserves this introduction.
Consider an illustrative comparison. A painter draws a hand before painting it. A sculptor studies its joints before carving it. An architect sketches how parts will fit together. The finished objects differ, but each task requires choices about relationships before those choices become a finished work. This comparison explains the shared principle; it is not an exercise assigned by Vasari.
The emphasis also raises the artist’s status. If making art requires judgment and invention, the artist deserves recognition for intellectual work as well as manual skill. Reading the book with this in mind makes its detailed attention to individual achievement easier to understand.
From correct construction to convincing ease In the preface to the third part, Vasari describes advances in rule, order, proportion, drawing, and manner. These establish sound construction. But correct construction alone does not produce the highest art.
He values a further quality of grace and freedom. A figure can have the right proportions yet look stiff. A master must make the body seem alive without making every anatomical lesson obvious. Knowledge should support the effect rather than overwhelm it.
His idea of a beautiful manner also involves selection. Artists study beautiful parts of nature and bring them together. Art therefore does more than copy an object exactly as it happens to appear.
For a viewer, this suggests two separate questions. Does the image make its forms and space clear? Does it make them feel effortless and alive? The questions can reveal differences that the single word “realistic” hides. They remain useful even when we reject Vasari’s ranking of whole periods.
Giotto and the story of natural talent Vasari tells how Cimabue discovered the young Giotto drawing a sheep while tending a flock. The boy supposedly learned directly from nature before formal training. Cimabue recognized his ability and brought him to Florence. In Vasari’s telling, the pupil then surpassed the master’s manner.
The life of Giotto makes this anecdote serve a larger claim. Artistic renewal begins when exceptional talent looks closely at the visible world. A biography becomes a small version of the book’s whole history.
The useful distinction is between a story’s meaning and its proof. This account shows what Vasari wanted natural talent to look like. It should not become an established childhood event simply because the scene is memorable. Before using an anecdote as historical evidence, ask what independent support it has.
That reading method preserves the book’s literary force without giving every vivid detail equal authority.
Raphael: excellence has a social life Vasari’s portrait of Raphael connects achievement with conduct toward other people. He praises Raphael’s courtesy and the harmony among those who worked with him. The artist’s example makes collaboration part of artistic excellence. The Raphael selections in this primary-source reader show how closely Vasari links character and reputation.
This broadens the book beyond the image of a solitary genius. Works depend on relationships among teachers, pupils, assistants, and patrons. The person who can sustain cooperation has a different kind of power from the person who can only execute a brilliant passage alone.
A practical implication follows, although Vasari does not frame it as a modern management lesson. When studying a major work, ask who made its production possible. An individual name can help us follow a career while concealing the labor around it.
Vasari’s moral portraits also need scrutiny. Admiration for an artist’s work can make an attractive account of the person’s character seem more certain than the evidence allows.
Michelangelo as culmination—and a clue to bias Michelangelo embodies Vasari’s highest ideal because he excels in sculpture, painting, and architecture. The David, the Sistine ceiling, and his architectural work allow Vasari to gather the three arts into one career. The biography opens by presenting his gifts as a divine answer to earlier artists’ struggles.
The same volume’s life of Titian exposes the limits of that ideal. Vasari recounts a visit with Michelangelo to see Titian’s Danaë. He reports praise for its color, followed by criticism of Venetian training in drawing.
The contrast reveals a standard of judgment that favors the Florentine tradition. We can take Titian’s color seriously without accepting that it needs to be completed by a different school’s priorities. Vasari’s praise and criticism tell us about the works, but also about the values he brings to them.
What to keep, and what to question The book’s strongest contribution is its attention to change. A style has a history. People learn from predecessors, adapt methods, compete for recognition, and work within particular opportunities. Looking closely at individual careers makes those processes visible.
Its larger story is more restrictive. A single path toward perfection leaves little room for art pursuing other purposes. A flat devotional image, for example, may seek clarity or sacred presence rather than bodily illusion. Judging it only by Vasari’s preferred destination can obscure what it achieves. This is a limitation of his framework, not a claim that skill and observation never matter.
His selection of lives creates another boundary. The mostly male sequence can make artistic history seem narrower than it was. Vasari does include the sculptor Properzia de’ Rossi, but an exceptional inclusion cannot provide a full account of women’s opportunities or work.
Use the Lives beside images and independent historical research. First identify what Vasari praises. Then look for the visible feature that supports his judgment. Finally, ask what his standard leaves out. This approach treats him as an unusually revealing guide whose own position also deserves examination.
Sources National Gallery: Giorgio Vasari and Oxford University Press: The Lives of the Artists: author, editions, and three-age structure. Vasari, Gaston du C. de Vere translation: Volume I, including Giotto, Volume II, second-part preface, and Volume IV, third-part preface. Vasari: Volume V, Properzia de’ Rossi, and Volume IX, Michelangelo and Titian. Vasari excerpts hosted by Winthrop University: third-part preface and Raphael selections. Vasari on Technique, translated by Louisa S. Maclehose, edited by G. Baldwin Brown: technical introduction and disegno.
